(Section)

Among these is His, glorified be He, oath: ﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾, the constellations through which the sun and the moon pass. It has been explained as referring to the stars, or a kind of them, and it has been explained as referring to the great palaces. All of this is from the signs of His power and the proofs of His oneness. For the sky is a sphere whose parts are alike, and in a spherical shape no side is distinguished from another by length, shortness, or position; rather, its sides are equal. So His placing these constellations on this sphere, differing in their forms, shapes and measures, is impossible to have come into existence without an agent, and it is impossible that its agent be not able, not knowing, not willing, not living, not wise, or not separate from the thing made. This and the like demolish the foundations of the naturalists, the atheists, and the philosophers, who do not affirm for the world a Lord who is distinct, powerful, acting by choice, knowing its details, wise, and managing it.

So the constellations of the sky are its stations, or the stations of the planets within it, which are among the greatest of His signs, glorified be He. Therefore He swore by them along with the sky. Then He swore by ﴿the promised day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. It is both the thing sworn by and the thing sworn about, just as the Qur'an is sworn by and sworn about. It also indicates the occurrence of the promised day, on which all the messengers agree, and what His servants know of His wisdom and might, which refuses to leave them neglected or to create them in vain, and by other signs and proofs by which He, glorified be He, is shown to be possible, and at other times to be occurring, and at other times to be free from what His enemies say, that He will not bring it. So swearing by it, for one who believes in God, is like swearing by the sky and other observed existents.

Then He, glorified be He, swore by the witness and the witnessed, unrestricted and unspecified. The most comprehensive meaning of it is that He is the perceiver and the perceived, the knower and the known, the seer and the seen. This is the most fitting meaning for Him, and whatever else has been said is mentioned as an example, not as a restriction.

If it is asked, what is the connection between these three things sworn by? It is said: they are, praise be to God, in the utmost connection, and the oath by them encompasses every existent in this world and the Hereafter, and each of them is an independent sign indicating His lordship and divinity. So He swore by the upper world, which is the sky and what is in it of constellations, the greatest and most spacious of places. Then He swore by the greatest and most magnificent of days, which is the manifestation of His kingdom, His command and prohibition, His reward and punishment, the gathering place of His allies and enemies, and the judgment between them by His knowledge and justice. Then He swore by what is more general than all of that, which is the witness and the witnessed. This oath is suitable to the mention of the People of the Trench, who tortured His allies, and they are witnesses to what is done to them, and the angels are witnesses against them concerning that, and the prophets, and their own limbs bear witness against them. Also, the witness is the one who observes, the watcher, the informer, and the witnessed is the one who is observed, informed about, and seen.

So from the type of creation there is a witness and a witnessed, and He is the most capable of the capable, just as He divided it into what is seen by us and what is unseen, as He said: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see﴾. Just as He divided it into earth and sky, night and day, male and female, this variety and difference is among His signs, glorified be He; likewise He divided it into witness and witnessed.

There is also another secret in it: among the created beings there is that which is witnessed against, and the order of the world is not complete except by this. How could a created being be a witness, watcher and guardian over another, while the Creator, blessed and exalted be He, would not be a witness over His servants, observing them and watching over them?

Also, this includes an oath by His angels, prophets and messengers, for they are witnesses over the servants, so it falls under the category of the sworn-by and the sworn-about being united, as He swore by the promised day, which is both the thing sworn by and the thing sworn about. Also, the Day of Resurrection is witnessed, as Almighty God said: ﴿That is a day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a day witnessed﴾, witnessed by God, His angels, humans, jinn, and wild beasts, which are among His signs, and the witnessed is among His signs.

Also, His speech is witnessed, as Almighty God said: ﴿And the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, witnessed by the angels of the night and the angels of the day. So the witnessed is among His greatest signs, and likewise the witness. Thus everything to which the name witness and witnessed applies is included in this oath, and there is no basis for restricting it to some of the types or specific things except as an example.

Also, the book of the righteous in ʿIlliyyin is witnessed by those brought near, so the book is witnessed and those brought near are witnesses.

It is best that this oath be without a response (jawab), because the purpose is the drawing of attention to the thing sworn by, and that it is one of the great signs of the Lord. It is unlikely that the response is ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾, who persecuted His allies and tortured them with the fire full of fuel.

Then He described their ugly condition: that they were sitting by the edge of the trench, witnessing directly what was being done to the servants of God and His allies, and mercy or compassion did not move them. They did not blame them for any religion except their belief in God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, to whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.

This description calls for honoring them, magnifying them and loving them, yet they treated them in the opposite manner to how they should have been treated. This is the way of God's enemies always: they resent in God's allies what they ought to be loved and honored for, as Almighty God said: ﴿Say, O People of the Scripture, do you resent us except that we believe in God and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?﴾

Likewise the people of Lot resented God's servants for their purity from the like of their deed, so they said: ﴿Expel them from your town; indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾.

Likewise the polytheists resent from the monotheists their devotion to the oneness of God, and sincerity of call and worship to God alone. Likewise the people of innovation resent from the People of the Sunnah their adherence to it and abandoning what contradicts it. Likewise the Mu'attilah (deniers of divine attributes) resent from the People of Affirmation their affirming to God the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty. Likewise the Rafidah resent from the People of the Sunnah their love for all the Companions, their being pleased with them, their allegiance to them, their preference for those whom the Messenger of God preferred, and their placing them in the ranks where God and His Messenger placed them. Likewise the people of newly invented opinion resent from the People of Hadith and the party of the Messenger their adherence to his hadith and their abandoning whatever contradicts it. All these have a share in it, and there is a resemblance between them and the People of the Trench, and between them there is a close or distant kinship.

The wonder is at al-Farisi (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, the grammarian), who says, regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿the fire, full of fuel﴾, that it is a substitute (badal) for "al-Ukhdud" (the trench) in the manner of badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), while the fire is a substance that subsists by itself. Moreover, it is not attributed to a pronoun referring back to "al-Ukhdud," and there is none of the conditions of badal al-ishtimal in it. Abu 'Ali overlooked this and abandoned what is more correct in meaning and more fitting to the discipline of grammar (sina'at al-nahw), which is the deletion of the modified noun (al-mudaf) and the placing of the modifying noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) in its position. So it is as if it were said: "the people of the trench, the trench of the fire, full of fuel," and thus it is a substitution of one thing for another while both refer to one and the same entity, as the poet said:

"My foster-brothers from the milk of a breast, or did they swear an alliance?"

According to the reading with the genitive (jarr) on "thady" (breast), either he meant "milk of a breast" and deleted the modified noun.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 85, verse 10:

Then He, glorified is He, informed that He has prepared for them the punishment of Jahannam (Hell) and the punishment of the Burning, because they did not repent, and that if they had repented after they tormented His friends (awliya') and punished them with fire, He would have forgiven them and not punished them.

And this is the utmost of generosity and munificence.

Al-Hasan said: "Look at this generosity and munificence! They kill His friends and torment them, and He calls them to repentance and forgiveness."

Look at the generosity of the Lord, exalted is He: He calls them to repentance, though they tormented His friends and burned them with fire. So a servant should not despair of His forgiveness and pardon, however much he may have done. There is no enmity greater than this enmity, and no disbelief more severe than that of one who burns with fire someone who believed in Allah alone and worshipped Him alone. Yet, even so, if they repented He would not punish them, and He would join them to His friends.

And he said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn):

Some of the early generation (al-salaf) said: "Look at His generosity: how they tormented His friends and burned them with fire, and yet He calls them to repentance!"

This is a door through which every person may enter to the love of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for His blessings upon His servants are witnessed by them, and they move within them with every breath and every moment.

(Benefit)

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent﴾

Here, "fitnah" has been interpreted as their punishing the believers and burning them with fire, but the word is more general than that.

Its essential meaning is: they tormented the believers so that they would be turned away from their religion. This is the fitnah attributed to the polytheists.

As for the fitnah that Allah, glorified is He, attributes to Himself, or that His Messenger attributes to Him, such as His saying: ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others﴾ [al-An'am: 53], and the saying of Musa: ﴿It is but Your trial; You send astray thereby whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], that is with another meaning. It means testing, examination, and trial from Allah of His servants with good and evil, with blessings and calamities. This is one kind; the fitnah of the polytheists is another kind; and the fitnah of a believer in his wealth, his children, and his neighbour is yet another kind.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the reward of His believing friends (awliya'). Then He mentioned the severity of His seizing (batsh) and that nothing can overpower Him, for He is the One who originates and restores (al-mubdi' al-mu'id). Whoever is like this, none is more severe in seizing than Him. Yet at the same time He is al-Ghafur (the All-Forgiving) al-Wadud (the Most Loving). He forgives whoever repents to Him, loves him (yawaddu-hu) and cherishes him (yuhibbu-hu). So He, glory be to Him, is described with severity of seizing, and yet He is al-Ghafur al-Wadud, the one who shows affection (al-mutawaddid) toward His servants through His blessings, who loves whoever repents to Him and turns to Him. He is also al-Wadud in the sense of al-mahbub (the one who is loved). Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "al-Wadud is al-Habib (the Beloved)." The verified position is that the word indicates both matters: that He is a lover (wadud) to His friends and one who is loved (mawdud) by them. The first is by the lexical form (bi'l-wad') and the second by necessary implication (bi'l-luzum). So He is the Beloved, the one who loves His friends; He loves them and they love Him.

And Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.﴾

How subtle is the pairing of al-Wadud with al-Rahim and al-Ghafur. A man may forgive one who has wronged him without loving him, and likewise he may show mercy to one he does not love. But the Lord, exalted is He, forgives His servant when he repents to Him, shows mercy to him, and loves him besides that, for He loves those who repent (al-tawwabin). When His servant turns back to Him, He loves him, no matter what had come from him.

(Section)

Know that sin is like sickness, and repentance is like health. When a servant falls ill and then recovers, and his health is fully restored, his condition returns to what it was, and may even return stronger and more complete than it was before. For in a state of health there may have been hidden pains and latent ailments, and when he falls ill these ailments appear, and then they are entirely removed by restored health, so his strength returns better than it was and more complete.

To this effect a poet said:

Perhaps your rebuke has a praiseworthy outcome,
and bodies are often made healthy through illnesses.

This is one of the reasons adduced by those who say that the servant returns, through repentance, to something better than what he was before repenting.

They also argued for their view that repentance yields for the servant a special love from Allah which is not attained without repentance; repentance is a condition for its attainment. Even if he gains another love through other acts of obedience, the love gained through repentance is not reached by any other means, for Allah loves those who repent (al-tawwabin), and among the signs of His love for them is that His joy at the repentance of one of them is greatest and most complete.

When repentance bears this love for him, and he returns with it to the acts of obedience he was performing earlier, its effect joins the effect of those acts, and the two effects strengthen one another, so he attains more closeness and nearness. This is contrary to the view held by one whose knowledge of his Lord is deficient, that when Allah forgives His servant's sin, the affection He had for him before the transgression does not return.

In support of this they cited a false Israelite report (athar isra'ili) that Allah said to Dawud (peace be upon him): "O Dawud, as for the sin, We have forgiven it; as for the affection, it will not return."

This is certainly a lie. Affection returns after sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) greater than it was, for He loves those who repent. Were the affection not to return, His love for him would not be attained. Moreover, He rejoices at the repentance of the penitent, and it is impossible that He rejoice in it with the greatest and most complete joy while not loving him.

Reflect on the secret of the pairing of these two names in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats. And He is the Forgiving, the Loving﴾ [al-Buruj: 13-14].

You will find in it a refutation and rejection of those who say that the affection and love of Him for His servant never return, which is among the treasures of the Qur'an and the subtleties of its understanding. In it is that which stirs the sound heart, seizes its very core, and makes it devoted to its Lord, He besides whom there is no god and no lord, with the devotion of the sincere lover to his beloved, whom he cannot do without, whose need he cannot avoid, and whose necessity cannot be met by anything else at all.

Then He said, ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾. He attributed the Throne to Himself, as great and noble things are attributed to Him, and this indicates the greatness of the Throne and its nearness to Him, glory be to Him, and its special relationship with Him. Indeed, it indicates the utmost nearness and special relationship, just as He attributes to Himself those who possess His attributes that subsist in Him, as in His saying: ﴿Possessor of strength, Possessor of majesty and honour﴾. It is also said: Possessor of might (dhu al-'izzah), Possessor of dominion (dhu al-mulk), Possessor of mercy (dhu al-rahmah), and similar expressions. So if the Throne's share of Him were the same as the share of the seventh earth, there would be no difference between saying "Lord of the Throne" and "Lord of the earth."

Then He described Himself as ﴿Glorious (al-majid)﴾, which includes the abundance of His attributes of perfection, their vastness, the inability of creation to count them, the vastness of His acts, and the abundance and permanence of His goodness. As for one who has no attributes of perfection and no praiseworthy acts, he has no share of glory at all. A created being becomes glorious only through his attributes and acts. So how could the Lord, blessed and exalted, be glorious while He is devoid of attributes and acts? Exalted is God above what the deniers of attributes (al-mu'attilah) say, a great exaltation. Rather, He is al-Majid, the One who does what He wills. In the language of the Arabs, majd means the abundance of attributes of perfection and the abundance of acts of goodness. The best pairing of the name al-Majid is with al-Hamid, as the angels said to the household of the Friend (Khalil, i.e. Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾. And as He prescribed for us at the end of the prayer that we extol the Lord, exalted is He, as "Praiseworthy and Glorious," and prescribed that at the end of the rak'ah, at the rising from bowing (i'tidal), we say: "Our Lord, and to You be praise, the One worthy of praise and glory." So praise and glory absolutely belong to God, al-Hamid, al-Majid. Al-Hamid is the Beloved, the One deserving of all attributes of perfection, and al-Majid is the Great, the Vast, the Capable, the Self-Sufficient, Possessor of majesty and honour. As for the one who reads "al-Majid" with a kasra, it is an attribute of His Throne, glory be to Him. And if His Throne is glorious, then He, glory be to Him, is more deserving of glory. Some people have found this reading problematic and said: "al-Majid has not been heard as an attribute of created beings," and then they explained it as either a case of attraction (al-jiwar) or as an attribute of "your Lord." This is due to the scantiness of the merchandise of the one who says this, for God, glory be to Him, described His Throne as "Generous" (karim), which is a counterpart of glory, and described it as "Great" (azim). So describing Him as glorious corresponds to describing Him as great and generous. Indeed, it is the most deserving of creatures to be described thus, because of its vastness, its beauty, and the splendour of its appearance, for it is the vastest of all created things, the most beautiful, and the most comprehensive of the qualities of beauty, splendour of appearance, loftiness of rank, and essence. No one can measure its greatness, beauty, and splendour of appearance except God. Its glory is derived from the glory of its Creator and Originator. The seven heavens and the seven earths, compared to the Footstool (al-Kursi) that is before Him, are like a ring thrown into a desert waste, and the Footstool compared to the Throne is like that ring in the desert. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The seven heavens in relation to the Throne are like seven dirhams placed in a shield." So how could it not be glorious, when such is its condition? He is Great, Generous, Glorious. As for this one who strains himself, driving it toward attraction (al-jiwar) or toward being an attribute of your Lord, that is severe strain and a departure from what is familiar in the language without any need for it.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 85, verse 16**

His saying, ﴿Doer of whatever He wills﴾, is evidence of several matters.

The first is that He, glory be to Him, acts by His will and His volition.

The second is that He has always been so, because He has always been so. He stated this in the context of praising and extolling Himself, and that it is among His perfections, glory be to Him. It is therefore impossible for Him to lack this perfection at any time. He, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not be reminded?﴾

Whatever is among the attributes of His perfection and the qualities of His majesty cannot have come into being after not having been.

The third is that when He wills something, He does it. The word "whatever" (ما) is a general relative pronoun, meaning that He does everything He wills to do. This refers to His will as it relates to His own acts. As for His will as it relates to the acts of the servant, that has a different character. If He wills the act of the servant but does not will from Himself to enable him and make him its doer, the act does not come into being. If He wills it in the sense that He wills from Himself to make him its doer, then it comes into being. This is the subtle point that was hidden from the Qadariyyah (proponents of free will) and the Jabriyyah (determinists), and they went astray in the question of divine decree because they were heedless of it. There are two wills here: the will that the servant act, and the will that the Lord make him the doer. The two are not mutually necessary, although the first necessarily follows from the second but not vice versa. Whenever He wills from Himself to assist His servant and to create for him the means of the act, He has willed the act, and He may will the act for him without willing from Himself to create for him the means of the act, in which case the act does not come into being.

If this point is difficult for you to grasp and becomes unclear, then consider the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), relating from his Lord, that He will say to the servant on the Day of Resurrection: "I desired from you something easier than this while you were in your father's loins: that you should not associate anything with Me." That desire was not fulfilled, because He did not will from Himself to assist him in it and grant him success.

The fourth is that His act and His will, glory be to Him, are mutually necessary. What He wills to do, He does, and what He does, He has willed. This is unlike the created being, who may will what he does not do and may do what he does not will. Therefore, there is no doer of whatever He wills except Allah alone.

The fifth is the affirmation of a will that is multiple according to the acts, and that each act has a will specific to it. This is what is understood in human nature, and it is what people understand by will. His state, the Exalted, is that He wills continually and does whatever He wills.

The sixth is that whatever is suitable for His will to be related to may be done. If He wills to descend every night to the lowest heaven, to come on the Day of Resurrection to judge, to show Himself to His servants, to manifest Himself to them as He wishes, to speak to them, to smile upon them, and other things that He wills, glory be to Him, then nothing prevents Him from doing it, for He is the Doer of whatever He wills. The validity of this depends only on the report of the Truthful One about it. When He reports it, it is obligatory to affirm it, and rejecting it is a rejection of the perfection that He has reported about Himself, and this is pure falsehood. Likewise, if His will, glory be to Him, may erase whatever He wills and establish whatever He wills, then it is possible for Him to do it, and the will and the act are among the requirements of His sanctified perfection.

This surah, in its brevity, includes from monotheism the description of Him, glory be to Him, with might, which entails power and strength and the absence of any like; praise, which entails the attributes of perfection and transcendence above their opposites, together with His love and divinity; His possession of the heavens and the earth, which entails the completeness of His independence and the vastness of His dominion; His witnessing over everything, which entails the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of the outward and inward of matters, the encompassing of His sight over what is seen, His hearing of what is heard, and His knowledge of what is known; His description as severe in seizing, which entails the completeness of strength, might, and power; His being singular in originating and restoring, which entails the oneness of His lordship and His disposal of created beings in originating and restoring, and their submission to His power, so that nothing among them is beyond Him; His description as Forgiving, which entails the completeness of His generosity, kindness, independence, and mercy; His description as Loving, which entails that He is beloved to His servants and loving to them; His description as Lord of the Throne, whose true measure no one but Him can know, and that His Throne, which is specific to Him, is not fitting for anyone else to sit upon; His description as Glorious, which entails the vastness of knowledge, power, dominion, independence, generosity, kindness, and munificence; and that He is the Doer of whatever He wills, which entails His life, knowledge, power, will, wisdom, and other attributes of His perfection.

Therefore, this surah is an independent book on the fundamentals of religion, and understanding it is sufficient.

So all praise is due to Allah, who sent down the Book to His servant, and blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) to His servant.

(Benefit)

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned in *Kitab al-Mujabin* (The Book of Those Whose Supplications Were Answered), and in *al-Du'a'* (Supplication), from al-Hasan, who said: There was a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the Ansar, known as Abu Mu'allaq, who was a merchant trading with his own wealth and that of others, travelling with it through the horizons. He was devout and scrupulous. Once he set out, and a masked highwayman armed with weapons met him and said: "Put down what you have, for I will kill you." He said: "What do you want of my blood? Take the wealth." The robber said: "As for the wealth, it is mine, and I want nothing but your blood." He said: "If you refuse, then let me pray four rak'ahs." The robber said: "Pray whatever you wish." So he performed ablution and prayed four rak'ahs. Among his supplications at the end of his prostration was that he said: "O Most Loving, O Most Loving, O Lord of the Glorious Throne, O Doer of whatever You will, I ask You by Your might which cannot be overcome, and by Your dominion which cannot be wronged, and by Your light which fills the pillars of Your Throne, that You suffice me against the evil of this robber. O Helper, help me," three times. Then behold, a horseman came toward him with a spear held between the ears of his horse. When the robber saw him, he came toward him and struck him, killing him. Then the horseman came to Abu Mu'allaq and said: "Rise." He said: "Who are you, may my father and mother be your ransom? Allah has helped me through you today." He replied: "I am an angel from the people of the fourth heaven. When you made your first supplication, I heard a clattering at the gates of heaven. Then when you made your second supplication, I heard a commotion among the people of heaven. Then when you made your third supplication, it was said to me: 'This is the supplication of one in distress,' so I asked Allah to let me be the one to kill him." Al-Hasan said: Whoever performs ablution, prays four rak'ahs, and supplicates with this supplication will be answered, whether he is in distress or not.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 85, verses 19–20:

Then he concluded it by mentioning His action and His punishment of those who associated partners with Him and denied His messengers, as a warning to His servants against following their path, and that whoever does their deeds will be treated as they were. Then He informed about His enemies that they deny His Tawhid (Divine Oneness) and His messages, even though they are in His grip and He encompasses them. There is no worse state than that of one who opposes Him who holds him in His grip, who is able to act upon him in every respect and in every consideration.

So He said: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial, while Allah encompasses them from behind.﴾

This is the most astonishing of wonders: that one would disbelieve in the One who encompasses him, who holds his forelock, and who is able to act upon him.

This is the most astonishing of wonders: that one would disbelieve in the One who encompasses him, who holds his forelock, and who is able to act upon him.

Then He described His speech as majestic (majīd), and He is most deserving of majesty over every speech, just as the One who speaks it possesses all majesty. So He is the Majestic (al-Majīd), His speech is majestic, and His Throne is majestic.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "A glorious Qur'an" (﴿قرآن مجيد﴾), noble, because the speech of the Lord is not as the disbelievers say: poetry, soothsaying, and sorcery.

It has already been mentioned that majesty (al-majd) means breadth and abundance of good, and the abundance of good in the Qur'an is known only to the One who spoke it.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 85, verse 22:

His saying ﴿in a preserved tablet﴾: most of the readers read it in the genitive (majrur) as an attributive adjective (sifah) of "lawh" (tablet).

In it is an indication that the devils cannot descend with it, because its place is preserved from their reaching it, and it is itself preserved from the devil being able to add to it or subtract from it. So He, glory be to Him, described it as preserved in His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾.

He also described its place with preservation in this surah. So Allah, glory be to Him, preserved its place, and preserved it from addition, subtraction and alteration, and preserved its meanings from distortion, just as He preserved its words from alteration. And He appointed for it those who preserve its letters from addition and subtraction and its meanings from distortion and change.
